title: Crisis Analysis - DR Congo: Monthly Displacement Report, September 2025
content: In September 2025, a 65% decrease in displaced households was recorded in the eastern provinces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) compared to the previous month, with a total of 57,032 displaced households identified across North Kivu (23,153), South Kivu (21,220), Ituri (6,516), Maniema (5,537), and Tanganyika (606). Of the movements observed, 11.3% (6,420 households) represented returns to areas of origin, primarily in Lubero territory. However, armed tensions persist in M23-controlled areas, including Rutshuru, Masisi, Walikale, Lubero, and parts of South Kivu, where ongoing clashes between M23, VDP, Wazalendo, and FARDC forces—combined with airstrikes and territorial expansion—have driven new displacements, particularly in health zones of Masisi, Mweso, Pinga, and Kibirizi. Although a temporary lull allowed some return to Lubero, the overall trend remains one of new displacement and insecurity. In South Kivu, no returns were recorded, with only new displacements linked to conflict involving M23, FARDC, Raia Mutomboki, GuminoTwirwaneho, and local self-defense groups in Walungu, Kalehe, Kabare, Shabunda, and Fizi. In Ituri, continued violence from FARDC operations against the CRP militia (aligned with Zaïre armed groups) and CODECO-URDPC attacks on civilians led to new displacements without any returns. The situation remains highly unstable across the region.

title: RDC : deux attaques simultanées des ADF dans le Nord-Kivu
content:
The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) experienced two simultaneous attacks by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in North Kivu on the night of September 8–9, 2025. The first, the deadliest, struck the village of Ntoyo, located less than seven kilometres from Manguredjipa, the administrative centre of the Bapere sector in Lubero territory. According to Lubero’s military administrator, Alain Kiwewa, the assault was "a real carnage" with 71 bodies found, 14 houses burned and about fifteen wounded. The attack targeted villagers gathered for a funeral vigil, a tactic the ADF has used repeatedly. The violence sparked widespread anger, shutting down schools and economic activity in Ntoyo and Mangurejipa for the day.

The second attack occurred roughly 100 kilometres north, near Fotodu close to Oicha in Beni territory. At least 18 people, mainly farmers, were killed or wounded with a knife. The DRC and Ugandan armies have been conducting joint operations against the ADF, an insurgent group linked to ISIS, since 2021.

These incidents illustrate the ADF’s shift from ambushes in fields to attacks on public gatherings, heightening fear among local residents, as expressed by Laetitia Kamathe, who recalled a July 2024 church massacre that killed 43 people. The DRC army confirmed the attacks and visited the sites to reassure the population.

title: Crisis Analysis - DR Congo: Monthly Displacement Report, August 2025
content: The August 2025 displacement report for the Democratic Republic of Congo shows a 58% decline in displaced households compared to July, with 122,853 households recorded across the five eastern provinces. North Kivu led with 58,864 displaced households, followed by Ituri (39,640), South Kivu (15,223), Maniema (6,266) and Tanganyika (3,000). Of the total movements, 26.8% (32,864 households) were returns to places of origin, mainly in Djugu and Walikale territories. Persistent armed tensions under M23 control continue to fuel new displacements, especially in Rutshuru, Masisi and South Kivu, while North Kivu remains heavily affected by M23‑related instability. South Kivu experienced only new displacements, with no returns, largely due to clashes involving FARDC, FDNB, Mai‑Mai, M23, Gumino Twirwaneho, FNL and Red Tabara in the Highlands of Fizi, Uvira and Mwenga. In Ituri, new displacements stem from attacks by the CPR (Popular Convention for the Revolution) led by Thomas Lubanga, allied with the Zaïre group, against FARDC, while returns are encouraged by relative calm in Djugu. Tanganyika’s displacements are driven by clashes between Mayi‑Mayi militias (predominantly Bantu) and Twa militias amid a land conflict in Kayumba and Mwenge groupements (Manono territory).

title: Democratic Republic of the Congo - Eastern region: Overview of incidents against humanitarian workers (Jan - Aug 2025)
content: In August 2025, a total of '80 incidents' affecting humanitarian actors were reported, the highest monthly figure recorded this year, up from 28 incidents in June and 58 in July, indicating a sharp deterioration of security in eastern DRC since the third quarter. While the overall number of incidents targeting humanitarian personnel has increased, the most serious incidents—injuries, kidnappings, and killings—appear to have decreased, with only two kidnappings and two killings reported in August. The breakdown of incident types shows that intimidation, threats, and aggression accounted for 24 % of reported incidents, burglary, robbery, and intrusions represented the largest share at 39 %, and interference and restrictions made up 33 %. These figures highlight the growing exposure of humanitarian staff to direct confrontation and coercion by various parties to the conflict. North and South Kivu remain the provinces most affected, but incidents have also risen in Maniema and Ituri, underscoring a complex, context‑specific threat environment for humanitarian operations throughout eastern DRC.

title: Democratic Republic of the Congo - Eastern region: Overview of incidents against humanitarian workers (Jan - Jul 2025)
content: In July 2025, 57 incidents affecting humanitarian actors were reported in the Eastern region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, more than double the 27 incidents recorded in June. This sharp increase follows several weeks of decline, with most incidents concentrated in North Kivu and South Kivu. Between January and July 2025, 354 incidents against humanitarian workers were documented, with 169 in North Kivu province, 98 in South Kivu, 44 in Ituri, and 30 in Tanganyika. Access constraints remain severe, with strategic humanitarian axes such as Masisi-Walikale in North Kivu, Bukavu-Uvira in South Kivu, and Bunia-Fataki in Ituri being either blocked or heavily restricted due to insecurity and administrative constraints. According to ReliefWeb, 'Access to airspace remains limited, and cross-border movement with Burundi continues to face restrictions, disrupting aid supply chains and delaying the delivery of essential assistance.'

title: RDC : plus de 1,6 million de nouveaux déplacés enregistrés entre janvier et juillet (OCHA)
content: The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that more than 1.6 million new war‑displaced persons were registered in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) between January and July, bringing the total number of internally displaced people to 5.28 million. The provinces most affected are North‑Kivu, South‑Kivu and Ituri, which are described as the most unstable in the country. OCHA notes that over 50 % of the displaced civilians are women, and that 68 % of the movements were caused by attacks and armed clashes. In the past year, 86 % of internal displacement occurred in South‑Kivu (33 %), North‑Kivu (30 %) and Ituri (23 %), and 99 % of returns during the period were recorded in the same provinces. The report cites the M23 war in North‑Kivu, where camps formed around Goma were dismantled after the city fell, forcing people back into hazardous conditions. The M23’s advance into South‑Kivu and the fall of Bukavu in mid‑February led to thousands more displaced, some of whom sought refuge in neighbouring states. The Ituri province, also beset by local armed group violence, hosts additional thousands of internally displaced persons.

title: Rapport mensuel de déplacement, Septembre 2025
content: In September 2025, there was a 65% decrease in the number of displaced households in the five eastern provinces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) compared to the previous month, with a total of 57,032 households displaced. The Nord-Kivu province recorded the highest displacement with 23,153 households, followed by Sud-Kivu (21,220), Ituri (6,516), Maniema (5,537), and Tanganyika (606). Of these movements, 11.3% (6,420 households) represented returns to original locations, primarily in the Lubero territory. Armed tensions persist in M23-controlled areas, including Rutshuru, Masisi, Walikale, Lubero, and southern Sud-Kivu, continuing to drive new population displacements. Nord-Kivu remains the most affected province, with heavy fighting between the M23, VDP, Wazalendo, and FARDC in Walikale, Masisi, Rutshuru, and Lubero, compounded by aerial strikes and M23 expansion into new areas, leading to mass civilian displacement in health zones such as Masisi, Mweso, Pinga, and Kibirizi. Although a relative calm allowed partial returns in Lubero, overall instability remains high. In Sud-Kivu, only new displacements were observed with no returns, indicating ongoing instability, particularly in Walungu, Kalehe, Kabare, Shabunda, and Fizi, driven by conflict involving the M23, FARDC, Raia Mutomboki, GuminoTwirwaneho, and local defense groups. In Ituri, new displacements continue due to ongoing armed violence, including FARDC operations against the CRP militia led by Thomas Lubanga (allied with Zaïre) and CODECO-URDPC attacks on civilians across several groupings. In Tanganyika, displacement is primarily due to clashes between FARDC and Wazalendo triggered by disputes over mining revenue in the Musebe area.

title: République démocratique du Congo : Profil humanitaire - Nord-Kivu (janvier - juin 2025)
content: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, key humanitarian events have occurred since the beginning of 2025. Notable incidents include targeted assassinations and violence, arrests and threats, and armed violence in areas such as Walikale, Lubero, Goma, Masisi, and Rutshuru. Mass displacement has also occurred, with people returning to areas such as Nyiragongo, Rutshuru, and Masisi. Humanitarian access has been constrained due to road and infrastructure issues, suspended activities, and the closure of humanitarian offices. Additionally, a volcanic eruption occurred at Nyamulagira (Nyiragongo) in June, causing a lava flow towards the Virunga National Park.

title: Congo-Kinshasa: Principales tendances des violations des droits de l'homme en RDC - Juillet 2025
content: The United Nations Joint Office on Human Rights (BCNUDH) in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported 535 human‑rights violations in July 2025, a 6 % rise from the 506 recorded in June.  At least 87 % of these incidents occurred in conflict‑affected areas, with the North‑Kivu province accounting for 288 cases, South‑Kivu 118, and Ituri 56.  The majority of violations (72 %) were attributed to armed groups, notably the M23 with 234 incidents, Wazalendo with 48, the Allied Democratic Forces with 27, the Cooperative for the Development of Congo, and various Maï‑Maï factions each with 18.  State agents were responsible for 27 % of the documented violations, primarily military personnel of the Congolese Armed Forces (70 cases) and national police officers (48 cases).  The BCNUDH shares these trends with authorities to prompt judicial action against alleged perpetrators.
